body:
Meaning of Environmental Conflict

An environmental conflict arises when people, communities, industries or public authorities have competing interests or disagreements concerning the use, control, protection or consequences of environmental resources.

Environmental resources include land, water, forests, clean air and other natural systems. A conflict may involve disagreement over access to a resource, the distribution of environmental damage or the way a development decision has been made.

Environmental conflict does not necessarily mean that development must stop. It indicates that the benefits, costs or decision-making process are contested.

How Environmental Conflicts Arise

Consider a proposed industrial facility near agricultural land and a river. The facility may create employment and increase production. At the same time, nearby residents may fear pollution, farmers may be concerned about groundwater availability and downstream communities may be concerned about river-water quality.

The same project can therefore produce benefits for some groups and potential costs for others.

  • Competition for resources: industries, households and farmers may depend on the same limited water source.
  • Pollution and health concerns: untreated effluents or air emissions may affect people who do not receive the project's economic benefits.
  • Land-use changes: infrastructure or industrial expansion may affect housing, farming, grazing or access to common resources.
  • Unequal distribution of costs: one area may receive jobs or revenue while another bears significant environmental risks.
  • Exclusion from decisions: residents may object because they were not informed adequately or their concerns were not considered.

Who May Be Affected?

Affected groups depend on the type and location of the proposed activity. They may include nearby residents, farmers, fishers, forest-dependent communities, workers, small businesses and people living downstream or downwind of pollution sources.

Women, older persons, children, persons with disabilities and low-income households may experience particular difficulties in accessing resources or responding to environmental harm. Their concerns should not be assumed to be identical: different people may experience different effects.

Workers and local businesses may also depend economically on an activity that other groups oppose. Understanding these different interests is important for identifying practical and fair responses.

Environmental Justice and Fairness

Environmental decisions involve at least 2 questions:

  • Who receives the benefits and bears the costs? This concerns fairness in the distribution of jobs, services, pollution, resource access and other effects.
  • Who has a meaningful opportunity to participate? This concerns fairness in the process of making the decision.

A project does not become fair merely because total economic benefits are large. Serious harm concentrated on a vulnerable community still requires assessment and an appropriate response.

Public Consultation

Public consultation is a process through which relevant people can receive information, express concerns, suggest alternatives and provide views before an authority makes or finalises a decision.

Meaningful consultation should provide understandable information about the proposal and its likely impacts. It should allow affected people to raise concerns about water use, pollution, livelihoods, safety and possible measures to reduce harm.

Consultation is more useful when it occurs before important decisions become irreversible. Authorities should examine the information received and explain how relevant concerns have been addressed.

Public Hearings and Environmental Impact Assessment

Under India's Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006, as amended, specified categories of projects require prior environmental clearance. For projects subject to the public-consultation stage, this generally includes a public hearing organised through the relevant State Pollution Control Board or Pollution Control Committee and an opportunity for written responses.

Not every project requires an EIA public hearing. Legal requirements depend on the project's category and applicable provisions, including exemptions. Participation also does not automatically amount to a legal veto over the project.

Consultation helps decision-makers consider environmental and social concerns. Where a project proceeds, the applicable conditions and safeguards still need to be implemented and monitored.

Role of Institutions

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) performs national pollution-control functions. State Pollution Control Boards, including the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB), exercise relevant regulatory and monitoring functions within their jurisdictions. Urban local bodies have responsibilities relating to municipal services such as sanitation and solid waste management.

These roles are related but not identical. A municipal body providing waste collection is not the same institution as a Pollution Control Board regulating pollution under applicable laws.

Prelims focus

  • Environmental conflict can concern resource access, pollution, land use or unequal impacts.
  • Affected groups may include workers, residents, farmers and downstream communities.
  • Fairness concerns both distribution of impacts and participation in decisions.
  • The EIA Notification, 2006 provides a public-consultation framework for specified projects.
  • GPCB is Gujarat's State Pollution Control Board.
  • Trap: Public consultation is not automatically required for every activity and does not, by itself, confer an unrestricted veto.

[Sources: NCERT, Social and Political Life III, Class 8, Chapters 9 and 10, Public Facilities and Law and Social Justice; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, Chapter 12, Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems, printed pp. 135–139; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Environmental Impact Assessment Notification, 2006, provisions on public consultation, as amended and consulted 2 November 2026; United Nations, SDG Target 11.3, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Project information leads to applicable public participation, which identifies concerns for decisions, safeguards and monitoring without automatic veto power.

title: Environmental Conflict: Competing Interests, Affected Groups and Consultation

body:
Meaning of Just Transition

Environmental protection sometimes requires changes in how energy is produced, how factories operate or how cities manage transport and waste. These changes may reduce pollution but can also affect existing jobs, business activities, household incomes and local communities.

A just transition is a shift towards a more environmentally sustainable economy carried out in a manner that promotes decent work, social inclusion and fairness for the people affected by the change.

It recognises that environmental progress and social well-being must be pursued together. A cleaner technology may benefit society as a whole while creating difficulties for particular workers or communities. Those difficulties need to be considered rather than ignored.

Why a Transition Can Create Unequal Effects

Consider a region where many households depend directly or indirectly on a conventional energy industry. If that industry contracts as cleaner energy sources expand, some workers may lose employment.

Other local people can also be affected. Transporters, repair workshops, small shops and service providers may depend on the spending and business activity generated by the industry.

At the same time, cleaner industries may create new jobs. However, these new opportunities may require different skills or be located elsewhere. A worker who loses employment is not automatically able to enter a newly created occupation.

The purpose of a just transition is to reduce such avoidable hardship and help affected people participate in the benefits of environmental change.

Principal Elements of a Just Transition

Skills and Employment Support

Training and retraining can help workers develop skills relevant to changing industries. Employment support may include helping workers identify alternative work or access suitable new opportunities.

Reskilling means learning skills for a different occupation or role. It is different from merely introducing new technology into an existing workplace.

Social Protection

Some workers and families may require income support or access to social-security measures during a period of employment change. The type and availability of support depend on the applicable programmes and circumstances.

Training alone may be inadequate if a displaced worker cannot meet immediate household needs or if suitable jobs are unavailable locally.

Participation and Social Dialogue

Social dialogue involves discussion and negotiation among relevant parties about economic and employment decisions.

In the International Labour Organization (ILO) framework, the principal tripartite constituents are governments, employers and workers. A just transition also requires attention to affected local communities and groups whose interests may not be fully represented through formal employment relationships.

Inclusive Community Development

A transition should consider local livelihoods, access to affordable services and the circumstances of vulnerable groups. Workers in informal employment and businesses dependent on a changing industry may need particular attention.

This does not guarantee that no job will ever be lost. It means that the consequences of change should be anticipated and addressed through fair measures.

International Labour Organization Guidance

The ILO adopted its Guidelines for a Just Transition towards Environmentally Sustainable Economies and Societies for All in 2015. The guidelines connect environmental sustainability with decent work, social protection and social dialogue.

The central principle is that moving towards a greener economy should provide opportunities for workers and communities while addressing the adverse consequences that can arise during the change.

Environmental Conflict and Just Transition: The Distinction

ConceptCentral questionExample
Environmental conflictWhose interests or claims about environmental resources and impacts are competing?Residents and industry disagree over water use or pollution risks.
Just transitionHow can a shift towards cleaner activities protect affected livelihoods and distribute opportunities fairly?Workers receive retraining and employment support as an older polluting activity declines.

The 2 concepts can overlap. A poorly planned transition may create conflict if workers lose income without support or communities are excluded from decisions. Meaningful participation can help prevent or reduce such conflict.

Connecting Sustainable Cities, Cleaner Industry and Fair Transition

The concepts studied in this subtopic apply at different but connected levels:

  • Sustainable cities: improve public transport, efficient buildings, water services, waste management and accessible green spaces.
  • Cleaner industry: prevent unnecessary resource use and pollution through better processes, while treating remaining harmful waste.
  • Just transition: manage the employment and community consequences of environmental change through participation, skills, support and fair decisions.

For example, replacing highly polluting urban transport with cleaner services can improve air quality. A complete policy also considers reliable and affordable transport for passengers, appropriate working conditions and opportunities for workers whose existing roles are affected.

Prelims focus

  • A just transition combines environmental sustainability with decent work and social inclusion.
  • The ILO issued its Just Transition Guidelines in 2015.
  • Social dialogue involves governments, employers and workers in the ILO's tripartite framework.
  • Reskilling, employment assistance and social protection can support affected workers.
  • Environmental conflict concerns competing interests; just transition concerns fairness during economic and environmental change.
  • Trap: The creation of green jobs does not automatically compensate every worker or community that loses an existing livelihood.

[Sources: International Labour Organization, Guidelines for a Just Transition towards Environmentally Sustainable Economies and Societies for All, 2015, sections on social dialogue, employment, skills and social protection; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11 Economics, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 171–173; United Nations, Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 12, target descriptions, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Sustainable cities, cleaner industry and just-transition support connect environmental improvement, resource efficiency and social inclusion as distinct objectives.
pictures.caption: Environmental improvement is most sustainable when efficient systems and fair treatment of affected people are pursued together.

title: Just Transition: Making Environmental Change Fair for Workers and Communities
